title: The Peasant Marey
text:
In 1876 Dostoevsky recalled a day during his years as a convict in Siberia. It was Easter week, and the prisoners were drunk, brawling and singing obscene songs. Disgusted, he went out of the barracks, where a Polish political prisoner muttered to him in French that he hated these bandits. Dostoevsky went back in and lay on his bunk, and a memory from his childhood came to him.

He was nine years old, on his father's country estate in August. He had wandered into a birch wood when, in the silence, he thought he heard someone shout, "Wolf!" He ran screaming out of the wood to a peasant plowing in the field. It was Marey, one of his father's serfs, a man of about fifty.

Marey stopped his horse and held the trembling boy. "Christ be with you, cross yourself," he said. There was no wolf; the boy had imagined it. Marey smiled at him like a mother, gently touched the boy's quivering lip with a finger black with earth, and promised to watch over him as he walked home. Every few steps the boy looked back and saw Marey still standing there, watching.

Lying on the plank bunk, Dostoevsky climbed down and looked at the faces of the convicts around him. Suddenly the hatred was gone. Any of these shaven, branded men, he felt, might be Marey.
lesson: One stranger's gentleness can change how you see a whole group of people. Remember that those who seem hostile may carry the same tenderness inside.
people: Fyodor Dostoevsky as a boy, the serf Marey
location: Omsk prison camp and Darovoye estate (modern Russia)
source: Fyodor Dostoevsky, A Writer's Diary (February 1876), The Peasant Marey
